considered.name: All-Uses Funding Surplus With Cash Buffer
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), DELTA(invt, 1))), lt), RATIO(che, lt))
considered.hypothesis: Cash consumed by inventory buildup is investment in every economically meaningful sense, so the funding surplus should net out fixed capital, acquisitions and working-capital investment together before being compared to the liability stock.
considered.reasoning: Each prior completion of the uses-of-cash numerator improved the evidence — adding working capital lifted the t-alpha from 1.93 to 2.26 and adding acquisitions lifted the FMB slope to +3.08 — but the two completions have never been combined inside the winning rank-composite structure. This tests whether the identity's power scales with its economic completeness or saturates.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Worst-Year Self-Funding Capacity
considered.hypothesis: A firm is financially resilient only if it could fund its investment out of internal cash flow even in its weakest recent year; the minimum over the last three years measures the trough of the funding state, which is what determines whether a covenant or refinancing event was ever triggered.
considered.reasoning: Averaging over three years (TS_SUM) diluted the one-year signal, and first differences carried nothing, which together suggest the informative feature is not the trend or the mean but the downside of the firm's own funding distribution. TS_MIN is the natural temporal analogue of the weakest-link logic and is the one time-series concept the archive has not tested on the winning construct.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Total External Capital Raised
considered.hypothesis: Rather than inferring the funding shortfall from the cash-flow identity, measure the financing actually obtained: firms simultaneously issuing equity and expanding their liabilities are dependent on external capital to sustain their investment programs and subsequently underperform.
considered.reasoning: Both legs individually produced significant FMB slopes (equity issuance -2.00, liability-financed capex -2.22) but neither produced a reliable negative alpha alone, and each captures only one side of the external financing decision. Pooling them in the rank-additive form that repaired the composite family tests whether the short side of the story is best expressed through observed financing rather than through the inferred cash gap.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Investment Survival Runway
considered.hypothesis: The relevant survival statistic is how many times over a firm's available resources — cash on hand plus operating cash flow — cover its committed near-term outflows, namely its capital program plus the liabilities falling due within the year.
considered.reasoning: Every successful signal so far subtracts investment from cash flow, which compresses two very different firms (a large-cash, large-capex firm and a small-cash, small-capex firm) into similar values; placing committed uses in the denominator makes the measure a coverage multiple that scales naturally and stays finite for firms with negligible liabilities. It combines the two channels of the leading composite in a single ratio without the skewness problem that ruined the additive-inside-ratio version.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Runway-Augmented Buffer Composite
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(che, oancf), ADD(capx, lct)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Coverage of committed near-term outflows by available resources and the surplus-after-investment relative to the debt stock are two non-redundant readings of the same resilience concept — one a multiple, one a margin — and pooling them by rank with the retained-earnings reserve should capture both the portfolio separation of the former and the linear cross-sectional slope of the latter.
considered.reasoning: The runway ratio produced the archive's largest alpha (+6.1%, t 3.71) but no FMB slope because it is a skewed multiple, exactly the pathology that rank pooling fixed once before when cash was moved out of the ratio and into a ranked channel. This directly merges the best-alpha construct with the best-slope construct in the aggregation form that has repeatedly repaired this problem.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Four-Buffer Resilience With Working Capital
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(re, lt), RATIO(wcap, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: Net working capital is a fourth, distinct financing reserve — receivables and inventory can be run down to fund operations without touching capital markets — so adding it to the flow surplus, cash stock and retained-earnings reserve should further separate firms that can sustain investment internally.
considered.reasoning: Each buffer added so far has raised the FMB slope (from +2.27 with two channels to +3.51 with three) while holding alpha near 5%, so the question is whether the buffer set has saturated or whether the working-capital reserve carries independent information. A null or diluting result would tell us the composite is complete and the final generations should refine weighting rather than add channels.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buffers With Current Profitability Reserve
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(ib, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: What protects a firm from its investment program is its current earning power relative to its debt burden, not the historical accumulation of past profits; substituting current income for retained earnings tests whether the third buffer works through present debt-service capacity or through accumulated cushion.
considered.reasoning: Retained earnings and current income are highly correlated but economically distinct — one is a stock of past success that may be stale, the other a flow that determines whether interest can be paid this year. This isolates a single channel substitution inside the leading composite and identifies which fragility concept the third buffer is really proxying for.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: All-Uses Three-Buffer Resilience
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(ADD(capx, aqc), DELTA(invt, 1))), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: The flow leg should net out every cash use that constitutes investment — fixed capital, acquisitions and working-capital buildup — before being compared to liabilities, so the most complete uses-of-cash definition combined with the validated buffer channels should dominate.
considered.reasoning: The all-uses numerator delivered alpha +5.2% with t 3.14 in the two-channel composite, and the three-buffer structure independently delivered the best slope and Sharpe, but the two improvements have never been combined. This is the last untested completeness dimension of the leading construct and should either confirm additivity of the two gains or reveal that inventory changes add noise once acquisitions are already netted.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Internally Sourced Buffer Composite
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), sstk), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: A surplus achieved only because the firm sold equity is not resilience; purging issuance from the flow leg leaves a measure of genuinely internal financing sufficiency, which should be the cleaner predictor of subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Netting issuance out of the simple identity preserved the slope (fmb +2.39) but has never been tested where it matters most, inside the composite whose long leg may currently be populated by cash-rich firms that raised that cash externally. If this improves the leader, the mechanism is internal self-sufficiency; if it weakens it, market access itself is part of the resilience being priced.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capital Program Relative To Liquid Reserves
considered.hypothesis: The most fragile expanders are firms whose annual investment program is large relative to the cash they actually hold and who have no accumulated earnings cushion behind it; such firms must return to capital markets within months to keep investing.
considered.reasoning: Every prior investment-intensity measure was scaled by assets or PP&E, which says nothing about financing capacity, whereas scaling the capital program by the cash reserve expresses it in units of survival time and is a functional form the archive has never tested. Pairing it with the retained-earnings reserve in additive rank form keeps both legs populated and gives a short leg of cash-poor, deficit-laden expanders that is economically homogeneous.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Earnings-Based Buffer Resilience
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Income before extraordinary items is an economically equivalent measure of the internal resources available to fund a capital program, so replacing operating cash flow with earnings should preserve the resilience mechanism while extending it to the large set of firm-years where cash-flow-statement data are unavailable.
considered.reasoning: Every leading signal is capped near 0.087 coverage because oancf is the binding constraint, while the one construct avoiding it reached 0.121 coverage with fmb +2.90; if the earnings-based flow leg retains the slope and alpha, we gain roughly forty percent more usable observations and a longer sample without changing the economics. A material deterioration would instead tell us that accrual-free cash generation, not accounting profit, is what the market misprices.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Flow-Weighted Multi-Horizon Buffer Composite
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lct), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(re, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: The funding-surplus channel carries more information than either stock buffer, so it should receive greater weight, and measuring it against both total and near-term claims captures solvency and rollover risk as separate readings of the same surplus.
considered.reasoning: The archive has only tested equal-weight channel pooling, yet the flow leg alone delivered fmb +3.08 while each stock buffer alone delivered less, implying the equal-weight composite underweights the most informative channel. Entering the surplus twice with different denominators doubles its effective weight while simultaneously testing the maturity-horizon question that gave fmb +2.49 in isolation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net-Liquidity Buffer Resilience
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Cash that is fully offset by debt maturing within the year is not a buffer at all; the true liquidity reserve backing an investment program is cash net of short-term borrowings, and netting them should remove firms that look liquid only because they have drawn credit lines.
considered.reasoning: The cash channel is what drives the composite's portfolio alpha, but gross cash misclassifies levered firms holding borrowed balances as resilient, precisely the firms the distress story says should be short. This is a targeted economic correction to the highest-alpha channel rather than another added buffer, which the four-buffer test showed to be unproductive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Internal Sufficiency With Earning Power
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), sstk), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(ib, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: The most reliable resilience portfolio combines a funding surplus that was not manufactured by selling equity with a cash reserve and demonstrated current earning power against the debt burden.
considered.reasoning: The two highest-Sharpe variants in the archive were issuance-netting (0.565) and the current-profitability buffer (0.465), and each addressed a different weakness of the leader — externally financed surpluses and stale accumulated cushions respectively. Combining them tests whether their Sharpe improvements are independent, which matters because the objective values reliability of the spread as much as its size.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Smoothed-Surplus Buffer Resilience
considered.expression: SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), 3), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Annual capital programs are lumpy, so a single year's surplus misclassifies firms in a heavy build year as fragile; averaging the surplus over three years measures the firm's normal self-funding capacity while the stock buffers remain contemporaneous.
considered.reasoning: The stock buffers are already persistent by construction, so the composite's turnover and noise come almost entirely from the lumpy flow leg, which is a plausible reason its Sharpe stops at 0.55. Smoothing only that channel is a precise design intervention, distinct from the earlier failed attempt that cumulated the flow while dropping the buffer channels entirely.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buffers With Capital Program Burn Multiple
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), che)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: How many years of investment the cash reserve can sustain is an investment-intensity measure expressed in survival time, and adding it explicitly ensures the composite ranks firms on the aggressiveness of their capital program relative to their resources, not merely on how much cash they hold.
considered.reasoning: The burn multiple standalone gave fmb +2.90 and t-alpha 3.00 on a much broader sample (coverage 0.121), and it is the only high-performing channel in which investment appears in the numerator rather than being subtracted from cash flow, so it is the least redundant addition available. It also replaces the gross-cash channel, which should reduce the composite's tilt toward simply cash-rich firms while preserving the liquidity information through the denominator.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Four-Channel Burn And Buffer Resilience
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), che)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lt), RATIO(re, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: Financial resilience against an investment program is fully described by four non-redundant readings — how many years of capital spending the cash reserve sustains, the surplus after all investment relative to debt, the cash stock relative to debt, and the accumulated earnings cushion — and pooling all four by rank should maximize both the cross-sectional slope and the abnormal spread.
considered.reasoning: The burn multiple raised alpha to +5.9% when it replaced the cash channel, and the cash channel independently drove the +5.8% alpha of the two-channel composite, so the open question is whether they are substitutes or complements — the burn multiple carries investment intensity in the numerator while cash-to-liabilities carries solvency. This is the direct consolidation of every channel that has independently earned its place.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Burn Multiple With Cash Buffer Ablation
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), che)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), RATIO(che, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Once investment intensity is measured against the cash reserve and the surplus is measured against liabilities, the accumulated retained-earnings cushion adds nothing incremental because it is already reflected in the firm's ability to hold cash and generate surplus.
considered.reasoning: This is the deliberate counterfactual to Signal 1 and identifies the marginal contribution of the earnings reserve rather than leaving it confounded, which matters because the four-buffer experiment in gen 7 showed channel addition can saturate and dilute. If this matches or beats the four-channel version, the simpler and more interpretable signal wins on parsimony at equal coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Burn Multiple With Multi-Horizon Surplus
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), che)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lct), RATIO(re, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: The funding surplus deserves double weight and should be read against both total and near-term claims, since solvency and rollover risk are distinct failure modes, while the burn multiple supplies the investment-intensity dimension and retained earnings the accumulated cushion.
considered.reasoning: Double-weighting the surplus across two horizons produced the best Sharpe among high-slope signals (0.560 with fmb 3.38) and the burn multiple produced the best composite alpha (+5.9%), and the two improvements act on different parts of the ranking. The risk is coverage dilution toward 0.076, which the accompanying proposals hedge against.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Internally Sourced Burn And Buffer Composite
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), che)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), sstk), lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm is resilient only if its investment is small relative to its own cash and its surplus was not manufactured by issuing equity; purging issuance from the flow leg while retaining the burn multiple should give the most stable spread of any specification.
considered.reasoning: Issuance netting produced the two highest Sharpes in the archive (0.565 and 0.544) by removing firms whose apparent surplus came from selling stock, and the burn multiple contributed the largest composite alpha; combining them targets the reliability dimension of the objective directly. If Sharpe rises above 0.57 while alpha stays near 5%, this is the best risk-adjusted version of the mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Burn Multiple With Current Earning Power
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), che)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), RATIO(ib, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Whether a firm survives its capital program depends on present debt-service capacity rather than a possibly stale stock of past profits, so current income relative to liabilities is the more forward-looking third channel alongside the burn multiple and the funding surplus.
considered.reasoning: Substituting current income for retained earnings in the three-buffer composite preserved the slope (3.45) and improved the Sharpe (0.465), indicating the two cushions are close but not identical proxies; it has not yet been tested alongside the burn multiple, where the interpretation shifts from cushion to debt-service coverage. This resolves which fragility concept the third channel should encode in the final specification.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Broad-Sample Burn And Earnings Buffers
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), che)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, ADD(capx, aqc)), lt), RATIO(re, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: The same resilience mechanism should be measurable on the much larger set of firm-years without cash-flow-statement data by using accounting income as the internal funding source, giving a version of the signal that is robust across the full sample rather than the post-1987 cash-flow era.
considered.reasoning: The earnings-based flow leg raised coverage from 0.087 to 0.121 while retaining fmb +3.07 and t-alpha 2.81, and its main weakness was a low Sharpe (0.255) that the burn multiple — itself estimable on the broad sample — is well suited to repair since it adds a liquidity dimension the earnings leg lacks. A strong result here delivers a signal whose evidence does not depend on the shortest and most recent portion of the sample.
considered.author: proposer
